Is Anyone There? Use of the Telephone and Use of the Couch

Lesley Murdin

Lesley Murdin

[lesleymurdin@gmail.com]

Lesley Murdin   Psychoanalytic psychotherapist who trained at WPF in London after obtaining a first degree in English literature and several years of teaching in Australia and the United States, as well as for the Open University in the UK. She obtained an MA in educational psychology at Sydney. She has published a number of books and papers, including How Much is Enough? on endings and How Money Talks. Her most recent book is on fundamentalism, Psychoanalytic Insights into Fundamentalism and Conviction. She chaired the UKCP Ethics Committee as well as the Analytic Section before it became a college. She chaired her Graduate Society, The Foundation for Psychotherapy and Counselling. She worked as National Director for WPF Therapy and has held positions at the BPC. She currently has a private practice in Cambridge
COUCH, TELEPHONE, TRANSFERENCE, SHAME, THERAPEUTIC FRAME, SEPARATION ANXIETY, RESISTANCE, LOSS

Many therapists have been using the telephone for analytic sessions during the Covid 19 pandemic. This paper considers the ways in which the use of the telephone resembles the use of the couch and revisits the value of the couch in order to assess the value of the telephone. The questions raised are whether analytic therapists still find the use of the couch helpful, and if so why. This is then linked to the experience of using only the telephone. The paper considers the ways in which the two techniques increase or diminish shame and the willingness to disclose difficult material. An anonymized clinical illustration is used of a woman who began in face-to-face work with a purely practical problem, but in telephone sessions was able to acknowledge her need to understand her own mental state in order to be able to change at a deeper level. Conclusions are drawn about the positive usefulness of the telephone in contrast with the view that it is just the best that we can do in some circumstances.

[[RunningHead]]

Rozsika Parker Prize 2021

The British Journal of Psychotherapy’s Prize established in 2013 in memory of Rozsika Parker focuses on a critical engagement with questions of creativity. An influential art historian and clinician, Rozsika Parker represented WPF/FPC on the BJP's Board for many years and was well known for her commitment to creativity, in both art and clinical practice. The Prize has two entry routes: a Student Path and a Post-Qualification Path. Students or qualified clinicians are invited to submit original papers on adult, child, couple, or group psychotherapy or psychoanalysis, on clinical, theoretical, applied or research topics. It is expected that authors will address the question of creativity in their submission, however broadly conceived. This may be implicit or explicit. In addition to the focus on creativity, the application of psychoanalytic theory to questions of gender; the arts; and social and cultural themes is welcomed. Authors should also consult the BJP‘s submission guidelines, particularly in relation to confidentiality and consent. Any clinical material must be fully anonymized, with disguise of any biographical details. The work should be prepared with the Journal's Aims and Scope statement in mind. Advice will be available for questions concerning confidentiality, or eligibility to submit work.

The Student path is open to students on an initial psychodynamic psychotherapy or clinical psychology or psychoanalytic psychotherapy training leading to a clinical qualification, who are either currently in training or who have qualified within the last 12 months; and to students on university courses in psychoanalytic studies, and on university courses where psychoanalysis is a significant component. The Post-Qualification path is open to clinically qualified individuals only. A paper that has only been made available to an institution's membership (for example, in an internal bulletin) is eligible to be entered into the competition, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers (Student or Post-Qualification) may have been submitted as part of the requirements of a programme of study, if this is acceptable to the author's course team, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers should be singly authored, but due acknowledgement should be made if the work is based on a joint project. Manuscripts should be between 4000 and 6000 words in length including references, not including an Abstract of 200 words which should head the paper. The word length must be stated on the title page. The author's name should not appear anywhere in the body of the paper. If the paper is based on or makes use of the author's earlier published work this should be acknowledged in the form ‘(Author, date)’ within the text (i.e. the word ‘Author’ is given, plus date of publication) and there should be no entry in the References list. Manuscripts should be sent as a Word attachment to Ann Scott, Editor-in-Chief, c/o the BJP's Editorial Administrator bjpsychotherapyadmin@wiley.com

[[RunningHead]]

Estela Welldon Prize

The British Journal of Psychotherapy is delighted to announce the establishment of the Estela Welldon Prize. Dr Estela V. Welldon worked for 40 years at the Portman Clinic in London as Consultant Psychiatrist and Consultant Psychotherapist. She is the Founder and Honorary President for Life of the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy, which, since its foundation, has held professional meetings every year in different parts of the world. Dr Welldon is the author, among many other works, of Mother, Madonna, Whore: The Idealization and Denigration of Motherhood, which challenged the traditional psychoanalytic theory that perversions are unique to males and which exposed the nature of female sexual offending. Creator of the world's first ever training course in forensic psychotherapy, in collaboration with the medical school at University College London, she has worked as both an individual and group practitioner for decades and continues to do so.

‘As a psychiatrist’, Dr Welldon has written, ‘I have spent my time contemplating the depths of the human psyche - sometimes in despair but usually in wonderment. As a forensic psychotherapist, I have continually been drawn to “the beauty hidden within the ugly”.’ She has often stated that every practitioner must search for the “golden nugget” of goodness and approachability within every patient, even those who seem unapproachable, such as certain forensic patients. The Prize, which is co-sponsored by the BJP and the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy, will be awarded annually to the author of a paper which contributes to our understanding of the shadow side of human nature - the ugly side, or what we might previously have called the ‘dark side’ of humanity. This might refer to acts of forensic violence, or cruelty in more intimate contexts. The Prize will be given to the paper which both illuminates the nature of human psychopathology in this area, and which reveals how the analytic clinician can overcome the obstacles and the challenges of therapeutic work to find that golden nugget.

He has practiced as a psychiatrist for over 50 years and has made significant contributions to the development of the Formal Theory, a wellness-based relational psychodynamic model, and the associated assessment, the Conflict Analysis Battery. ASSESSMENT, EVALUATION, INNOVATION, INTEGRATIVE PSYCHOTHERAPY, NONINTENSIVE PSYCHOTHERAPY, OUTCOME MEASUREMENT, PROJECTION, PROJECTIVE IDENTIFICATION

Assessment is a defining component of psychotherapy practice. Unfortunately, it is also a component that can be associated with heightened stigma, dropout, and financial burden. Responding to these concerns, Conflict Analysis (CA) was developed as a meaningful, accessible, and inexpensive online therapeutic assessment that can aid case formulation or function as auxiliary psychoeducation. CA is a client-led psychodynamic assessment that bridges diagnostic frameworks, therapeutic techniques, and technological resources. CA provides a diagnostic blueprint for subsequent interventions for little cost and from the convenience of clients' mobile devices. This study evaluates CA's perceived therapeutic and diagnostic utility through using a single-case research design, featuring the case of ‘Laura’, a 40-year-old African-American woman, randomly chosen from an online sample cohort. Authors had no direct contact with Laura. The study examines assessment responses, narrative writings, self-reflections, and self-report scores on measures predicting psychopathology, wellbeing, insight, and diagnostic and therapeutic benefits. Measures were evaluated before, immediately after, and two weeks after CA. Data suggest CA offered Laura insight into behavioural patterns and a growth framework. Laura indicated CA helped her balance between competing aspects of identity, and become more engaged, empowered, and open to therapeutic interventions. Findings should not be generalized as the study only presents an individual record.

When we differ on theoretical perspectives in psychotherapy, we regularly do so via appeals to the authority of the traditions we feel affiliated to or trained in, rather than a careful evaluation of the underlying philosophical presuppositions of those traditions. Such appeals to tradition frequently dovetail with the invocation of concepts we have a felt, clinical affinity for and find useful in our work, without over-concern for their philosophical warrant. For many of us I suspect, there's likely something of an ongoing, shifting mixture between the strength of identifications with the orientation(s) we trained in and/or now feel drawn to, the branching pursuit of fresh intellectual interests born of encounters with emerging clinical conundrums, as well as the evolution of a personal clinical technique.

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

[bob.hinsh@gmail.com]

Bob Hinshelwood  

Observation that includes the observer, as Sebastian Kraemer puts it, could be regarded as the hallmark of the Tavistock approach for which the Clinic is justifiably famous - in all the regions of the world. And that leads to a ‘sociatry’, a cure of social systems and not just of the individual psyche as it engages in society. The great advantage of the Tavistock is its continuous reflection on its organizational ‘self’ built into its renewal in 1945. This is a companion to Henry Dicks' (1970) volume on the first 50 years. Dicks ably wrote a workaday history of the first half-century, plotting the continuity up to 1970. The present volume overlaps, concentrating on the period after the Second World War when the Tavistock resurrected and renovated itself. Implicitly, this book seems to plot a discontinuity in which the eclectic founding tradition was built on, and perhaps built over, by the new ideas in the 1940s, mostly from psychoanalysis. Little reference is made to the first phase of the Tavistock, although Brett Kahr (Chapter 6) reviews the great and the good in London society who brought the Clinic into existence in September 1920 and supported it until it became the extraordinary specialist service incorporated in 1948 into the new National Health Service.

In the final afterword, Kraemer documents the post-WW2 resurrection - Operation Phoenix - fittingly published by the adventurous new publisher seeking to put psychoanalysis back onto the bookshelves. But Kraemer confides his growing sadness at the increasingly inclement context for the Clinic in today's society that hesitates uncertainly about the value of public service provision.

However, overall, this is less of a history and more of a celebration of the Tavistock's work in the last 50-60 years. That is to say, it is the work within the living memory of the authors of the chapters. Of course, that phenomenal amount of original work deserves celebration even though its constant innovation has sometimes been eccentric, sometimes conformist, sometimes reviled and sometimes revered. As Sebastian Kraemer, one of the editors, described it, ‘it is a patchwork of writings and recollections’ (p. 329).

Catriona Wrottesley  

Many books and papers have been written on the subject of interpretation, widely regarded among psychoanalytic practitioners as a principal (but not sole) agent of therapeutic change. The majority are from the perspective of individual psychotherapy and analysis. This volume, the 11th in the series ‘The Library of Couple and Family Psychoanalysis’ (begun in 2009), is different because it specifically focuses on interpretation in couple and family psychoanalysis from a cross-cultural clinical perspective. Co-editors Timothy Keogh from Australia and Elizabeth Palacios from Spain have brought together contributions from clinicians from the UK, Italy, France, Spain, North America, South America and Australia in order to debate within its pages the question of what kinds of interpretation in couple and family work may be transformative. The discussions found here originally took place at a conference in Madrid in 2017; the aim of publishing these papers now is to make that gathering's discussions accessible to a far wider audience and to provide a spur for advances in theoretical ideas and clinical practice that can emerge from this kind of creative dialogue.

The book's structure as well as its content demonstrates the editors' belief in the value of including a plurality of voices within the international field of couple and family psychoanalysis across the globe. It is divided into three sections. Part 1 examines interpretation within the field of psychoanalysis and how that may be applied to couple and family psychoanalysis; Elizabeth Palacios (Europe), Mary Morgan (UK), David and Jill Scharff (North America), Janine Puget (South America), Timothy Keogh (Australasia); Part 2 looks at the different ways in which interpretation is applied in couple psychoanalytic psychotherapy, and each chapter has two discussants - again with a range of international contributors (from the UK, Australasia, Spain, Argentina, Israel, France and North America); Part 3 focuses on family work, including a range of topics, such as the nature of family, social and intergenerational links, the arrival of a newborn, same sex couples' families, the bereaved family, and families with adolescent children.

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[bjp@ann-scott.net]

Ann Scott  

This time last year the BJP published two fast-track pieces on Covid-19 by international colleagues of the Journal: a ‘Letter from Northern Italy’ by Federica Facchin, and an interview with Gillian Isaacs Russell focusing on the sudden impact of the global situation on our work. Facchin brilliantly conveyed the shocking sense of the emergency in Northern Italy, while Isaacs Russell brought her longstanding expertise in computer-mediated psychotherapy to bear on the new, very difficult situation we were all in. They were among the BJP's most downloaded papers of 2020. So the Journal is both delighted and proud to be presenting their thoughts on the pandemic one year later. The sense of emergency has been replaced by a perhaps more sombre assessment of our evolving situation. Facchin's ‘Year of Sad Passions’ nevertheless carries a psychoanalytic ‘message of hope’, while Isaacs Russell puts her fervent commitment to co-present working in the context of her nuanced understanding of the remote working that the pandemic required.

We are again grateful to our publisher, Wiley, for making the papers free to access on the BJP pages on Wiley Online Library (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/17520118).

It is always a pleasure, in the August issue of the Journal, to present the winning papers in the Rozsika Parker Prize. In 2020 the Prize in the Student Path was awarded jointly, to two quite different but complementary papers, equally deserving of the award. Ros Howell offers a wide-ranging exploration of the ‘back and forth’ of time, combining her recent qualification in psychodynamic psychotherapeutic counselling with her earlier qualification in dance movement psychotherapy. In a sensitive exploration of her theme, which takes in both inner world and cultural context, and includes a number of succinct clinical vignettes, she suggests that ‘movement and bodily felt sensation and spatial awareness may illuminate different qualities of rhythmic temporality within the transferential and countertransferential relationship’. Daniel Weir explores ‘the discomfort that resulted from a brief exchange between a white male therapist and a black male patient’ that led to a breakdown in empathic communication. Discomfort is the guiding principle of the essay, allowing Weir to attend in depth and with honesty to ‘a particular moment that caused me to consider the impact of my whiteness upon my patient’, one in which ‘a dynamic was created in which difference was located not between my patient and me, but in my patient’. The focus on white racial experience is sustained in a reflective conversation between recent psychoanalytic work on internal racism and sociological work on white privilege.

Judith Trowell  

This is a slim book, but it packs in a great deal of information and research. It starts with a somewhat bland introduction that leaves one unsure, but then the first chapter is at once interesting and captures the attention. In this first chapter, Prophecy Coles explores three adoptions: Moses adopted by an Egyptian princess, knowing he was an Israelite; Ion abandoned by his mother and given to a couple who raised him not knowing his parentage; and then Oedipus and the unfolding story of his realization of his parentage and the implications of this. These three stories set the scene nicely for the psychoanalytic exploration of the complexity of adoption.

However, the author, before elaborating these, takes us on a journey from the sixteenth century in the UK, to reflect on what became of illegitimate children and their mothers. Adoption, if it occurred at all, was unregulated, very much a matter of chance. Prior to this in feudal England, they were taken into the community on the land where they lived and were expected to work.

In the sixteenth century when there was migration to the towns, mothers and their babies were left to flounder. In 1572 there was the first poor law, but unmarried mothers and their babies were not included in this provision. Mothers had to work and had to leave their babies, mainly in the workhouses where most of them died. This arrangement persisted for about three centuries. The author questions and explains that society feared ‘bastards’ (illegitimate children) would contaminate society introducing ‘bad blood’, and should be excluded or punished. Also, there was a belief that society should not interfere in the care of children in case the family were undermined. Those children that survived the workhouses were sold to work in the mines and factories.

Dr Barnardo then became involved. He started in the cities in the UK rescuing street children, setting up homes for orphans. Later in 1882, 150,000 were sent to the colonies, some as young as 4 or 5 years, to provide labour and civilize these countries! In 1889 the protection of children was instigated (the origins of the NSPCC) after in 1835 the protection of animals! At the end of the eighteenth century and in the early nineteenth century when soldiers were needed to fight wars, charities made provision for single mothers and their babies to be housed and fed so the boy children could go and fight.

This book is an impressive collection of papers on loss, mourning and melancholia. Although the book's focus is on couples and loss, it is highly relevant for clinicians working with individuals as well as families. Clinically useful theories are clearly

528

described, including some which may be new to UK readers. Many rich clinical examples illustrate the complexity of loss and confirm its central place in understanding human experience.

During the writing of this book, I suspect that the prospect of a pandemic, such as the one we are currently in, was very far from the authors' minds. Loss is everywhere, not only through the deaths of those young and old, but also due to the deleterious effects of the virus itself. Being unable to be with those who suffer or pay our final respects to the dying has added significantly to the complications and trauma of Covid. The pandemic has meant the loss of so many other aspects of our way of life, such as coming together with family, friends and colleagues; loss of jobs, income, cultural and sporting events, weddings and funerals. Published before the full extent of Covid and its variants could have been imagined, this book is even more timely because of the global crisis. One might say that uniting across the world has never been more necessary than now in this current pandemic, and in this regard, the book brings together authors who cross several continents, namely Europe, Australia and South America.

In terms of the book's theoretical stance, the chapters interweave object relations theory with the concept of the link or Link Theory, known as ‘El Vinculo’. This is a concept less familiar to UK psychoanalytic practice and likely to be new to some readers. The chapters course their way through many different aspects of loss, for example, the impact of loss through death, the ending of a relationship, loss of wishes and dreams, of youth, as well as the intergenerational aspects of loss. Clinical examples throughout the book illustrate how unacknowledged and insufficiently mourned losses give rise to complex mourning processes, which lead to problems for individuals in the couple relationship, the couple relationship itself, and for other family members.

What's American about American psychoanalysis? The question posed in 2004 in a special issue of Psychoanalytic Dialogues, and reprised at the January 2016 meetings of the American Psychoanalytic Association, has generated, amongst a good many other things, an interesting anthology of lectures, essays and occasional pieces by Nancy Chodorow, which have now been collected in The Psychoanalytic Ear and the Sociological Eye. The book provides a range of overlapping personal, professional and clinical reflections on how to articulate psyche and society, and how to reconcile the premise of ‘individuality’ with the mathesis universalis of modern thought. Chodorow is particularly exercised by the problem of how to put what she sees as the mutually hostile disciplines of psychoanalysis and sociology together, a preoccupation that relates to her own career as a professor of sociology and an analyst. There seems to be a never-failing urge to revisit this problem. More importantly, however, Chodorow's personal preoccupation points to the phenomenon of ‘hybridity’ in the history of psychoanalysis itself. In fact, I found the autobiographical narrative, which I felt was rather self-aggrandising at times, far less engaging than the wider theoretical and practical theme concerning the therapeutic integration of separateness and commonality, singularity and universality.

Chodorow considers psychosocial studies explicitly in the first part of the book. Her self-defined ‘hybrid location’, or ‘dual identity’ (social scientific and psychoanalytic), provides a point of departure for a discussion of Freud's ‘drive-based sociology’ (p. 24).

[annie.pesskin@gmail.com]

Annie Pesskin  

I am a passionate fan of neuropsychoanalysis, the ambitious attempt to understand ourselves from two contrary but necessary perspectives. Over the last two decades in a series of exciting international congresses, neuropsychoanalysis has offered a chance for neuroscientists, familiar with the cellular matter which makes up the neurobiology of our brains, to engage in dialogue with psychoanalysts who see this extraordinary 3 kg of matter from the perspective of a subjective mind in all the complexity of its sensations, thoughts, feelings and consciousness.

In this recent publication, Jeremy Holmes gives us all a handy introduction to one of the most fertile new strands of neuropsychoanalysis. His highly readable eight chapters, appended with an excellent glossary, concentrate exclusively on Karl Friston's (2009) free energy principle. Free energy is the force of entropy; unbound ‘free energy’ spells disorder and chaos for a biological agent, be it a single-celled bacteria or a human being. Thus, all living things must work to ‘bind’ this energy and minimize the entropy of their sensory states by maintaining homeostasis. In simple terms, when I find myself shivering, I put on a jumper. In grander schemes, the brain of every biological agent exists to ‘bind’ incoming information according to its predictive models of the world and they do so using the free energy principle. Mathematician Karl Friston has used Bayesian mathematics to show how human brains are engaged in using the free energy principle at every level of our functioning to keep entropy at bay. The reach of the theory is exciting and if you follow Holmes' thread by reading this book, I think you will agree he has done an excellent job of elaborating it.

Freud's earliest efforts to understand the mind in all its complexity was his unpublished 1895 Project (Freud, 1950) where he wrestled with the same mind/brain conundrum that researchers in neuropsychoanalysis attempt to bridge, but without access to all the findings of PET and fMRI scanners. Freud was a neuroanatomist before he invented the talking cure, after all. To see how Freud might have written the Project in 2020, have a read of Mark Solms' (Solms, M. 2020) updated version which is free to read, online.

Meg Harris Williams is a seasoned writer and literary critic and the latest Dream Sequences in Shakespeare: A Psychoanalytic Perspective is a perfect example of her talent and acumen. With a psychoanalyst and a poet for parents, her choice of psychoanalytic literary criticism is not surprising. Williams' psychoanalytic roots are steeped in the Post-Kleinian tradition (Money-Kyrle, Bion, and Meltzer; and of course their sources - Klein and Freud). A ‘dream’ has the meaning of phantasy (Klein). Dream-thoughts, to recall Bion's grid, are the basis of a preconception perceived by the unconscious. An attentive, observant mind can bring them to consciousness. The appendix spells out the post-Kleinian model of the mind with great clarity.

This book is about the imaginative creative process. It is also on Shakespeare's amazing capacity for insight into human nature. Williams' rigorous analysis of ideas is enhanced by her immaculate attention to the subtle and creative nuances and associations of Shakespeare's poetic language. She has previously written on Homer, Milton, Keats, Bronte, Ibsen, Kafka, to mention but a few. There is something additional, though, in the Dream Sequences in Shakespeare: the rich internal landscape that is founded on life-long immersion in the poet's work. She explains her approach in the preface:

This book explores Shakespeare's plays as dream-thought in the modern psychoanalytic sense of unconscious thinking. Through his commitment to poetic language the playwright discovers images and dramatic sequences that illustrate fundamental developmental conflicts whose solutions are not preconceived but evolve through the process of dramatization. (p. vii)

Fourteen plays are analysed in depth while others are often referred to as corroborative or conflicting. The order in which they are discussed is not chronological but, rather, they are presented in terms of stages in the emotional development of the protagonists. These are, in turn, a representation of Shakespeare's emotional and artistic development. Williams' perspective is psychoanalytic, engaging in development of the internal world, such as adolescent development (Richard II, Julius Caesar, Hamlet), the abhorrence of knowledge (Macbeth, Othello)

In the first issue of this volume of the Journal we were privileged to publish Estela Welldon's powerful meditation on living and dying, and to announce a Prize in her name, co-sponsored by the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy and the BJP. Now, as the year comes to an end, we are delighted to announce the winning and commended authors in the first year of the competition (p. 548). The papers by the joint winners, Stephen Blumenthal and Elena Mundici, will be published in the February issue of the Journal next year, and the paper by the commended author, Heather Wood, will be published next May. We warmly congratulate all three authors. I also want to thank my Editorial Board colleague Katya Orrell for convening and chairing the judging panel, and our anonymous judges for their valuable work.

Space does not permit me to do more than briefly acknowledge the rich work we publish in the final issue of this volume. Our Clinical Commentary reflects deeply on work with a mixed race man in his early sixties. ‘Violence followed him everywhere’, in the words of the clinician; our commentators look at technique and how the setting was managed (Laurence Spurling); the question of ‘to whom is the patient talking?’ (Cleo van Velsen); and the question of trauma (Richard Curen). In the November issue we always publish the commended papers in the most recent Rozsika Parker Prize. It is a pleasure to publish Emily Morgan's paper on education in the context of life-threatening illness (Commended, Student Path 2020), and Gaynor Maxwell-Scott's account of a forensic group for men (Commended, Post-Qualification Path 2020). Alina Schellekes then imaginatively considers early emotional development and primitive states. Joy Schaverien searchingly revisits Boarding School Syndrome, ten years after she first identified the syndrome, identifying different elements within it. In our New Voices strand, Anna Ellisin (a pseudonym) candidly explores the ‘hatred of learning from experience’ during clinical training. Our Clinical and Theoretical Practice strand ranges widely: papers cover the maternal uterus as the primary object (Panagiotis Kostaras); supervision and analytic culture (Hanoch Yerushalmi); social justice on the couch (Joachim Sehrbrock); the psychoanalyst as revolutionary (Alan Michael Karbelnig). Each of the four papers includes vivid clinical material.

David Henderson  

The quintessence is an important but under-theorised theme in analytical psychology. Christine Driver has done us the service of unearthing the references to the quintessence in Jung's Collected Works and of contextualizing the use of the concept in analytical psychology and beyond. The notion ‘comes from an ancient historic view of the world which considered that the essential spark of creation was hidden in matter and that this spirit in matter was the imago Dei (God)’ (p. 3). Like the idea of the transcendent function, it is a concept that appears marginal in Jung's texts but which upon closer investigation turns out to be ubiquitous in his theory. Driver describes her book as ‘a journey into the unknowable but also the known, as we experience an emergent understanding of what the quintessence represents’ (p. 13).

The first section of the book (‘Orientation, themes, and the symbolic significance of number’) discusses the role of number in philosophy, science, alchemy and psychoanalysis. ‘Numbers enable the identification of relational patterns and the patterns formed by one (unity), two (duality), three (triangularity), four (quaternity), five (quinity), etc., are symbolically significant’ (p. 4). Jung considered the quaternity to be an important image of wholeness and the self. However, it was also incomplete and needed be ‘united with the quinta essentia at the end’ (p. 17). The fifth represents both the beginning and end of a process.

Section two (‘Number as a symbol of psychological development’) has chapters on duality, triadicity and quaternity. Jung discusses the dynamics of the opposites extensively throughout his work. The tension of opposites is responsible for producing psychic energy. The play of opposites, or the lack of it, within the psyche accounts for aliveness and/or psychopathology. Driver alludes to binary dynamics in the thought of Klein, Fairbairn and Balint. She describes the importance of symmetry and asymmetry in the work of Matte-Blanco and Grotstein. ‘Duality is … a dynamic but results only in dichotomies and opposites, whereas the union of opposites results in a new element, a new perspective, leading to the opening up of more complex structures and interactive processes and perspectives’ (p. 38).

It is a great privilege to publish Estela Welldon's remarkable meditation on living and dying, a paper she has worked on over many years. Starting from her experience of sudden family deaths ‘from a young age’, she argues that ‘true awareness of death, including one's own, is life-enhancing and can inspire great creative acts’. The article is accompanied by a photograph that stages Estela's own ‘deathbed scene’, taken by her son, a professional photographer. Dan Welldon offers a revealing commentary on ‘the process by which I prepared to photograph my mother's deathbed scene’. Noting that a ‘reluctance to document death is a very recent phenomenon’, he identifies two main styles in earlier deathbed paintings: the ‘grand canvas’ and the intimate portrait of the artist's loved one. He chose ‘a synthesis of these two styles’ for the photograph; his commentary is accompanied by two further, memorable photographs of his mother.

With this issue we are also honoured to announce the establishment of a Prize in Estela Welldon's name. The Prize, co-sponsored by the BJP and the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy, ‘will be awarded annually to the author of a paper which contributes to our understanding of the shadow side of human nature - the ugly side, or what we might previously have called the “dark side” of humanity’. (For all the details, see p. 3.) The Estela Welldon Prize will complement our established Rozsika Parker Prize, which, as readers know, focuses on a critical engagement with questions of creativity in clinical or applied analytic work. I am very grateful to Brett Kahr and Carine Minne for their work in developing the Prize.

Turning to our regular Clinical and Theoretical Practice strand, we offer a rich group of papers. Hana Salaam Abdel-Malek explores the way in which her adolescent patient was able to ‘disengage from her internalized incestual family dynamics and the violence of an incestuous primal scene’. Nardus Saayman considers the psychotic patient's inability (at times) to ‘make sense of their subjective experiences in relation to an acknowledged other’. Leila Dubois-Barnes reflects on processes of ‘entrapment, invasion and phobic functioning’ inside and outside the consulting room, ‘as well as states of mind connected with safety and survival’, in a detailed case history. Satoshi Handa takes up ‘the difficulty for a therapist in accepting his mortality and the finiteness of things’, describing his period of sick leave for a serious condition and his inner conflicts on returning to clinical work; and the psychic resolution he was ultimately able to find.

Reading, let alone reviewing, this book was initially off-putting for me because of its ‘culture-breast’ title. It seemed too overly intimate or Klein-bound to me. Nevertheless, after working through this book's long and overly detailed first chapter, I found the issues it raises in its remaining chapters both innovative and relevant to psychotherapy.

Nor is its first chapter without interest. In it, as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist, Giffney highlights the tendency of psychosocial studies to focus, as Freud did in his book Totem and Taboo, on ways psychoanalytic findings can illuminate cultural issues. By contrast, she focuses on ways in which cultural objects, particularly from the creative arts, can be used to illuminate what occurs within the psychoanalytic consulting room so as to enable psychotherapists to work in increased psychoanalytic depth with their patients.

This brings Giffney to her book's second chapter. In it she draws attention to the value of infant observation in psychoanalytic training since, she says, it provides trainees with an ‘immersive and authentic experience to navigate and reflect upon’ (p. 69). This, she says, is due not least to the fact that it requires the trainee to recall and formulate their infant observation experience in writing process notes about it, in discussing it in small group seminars, and in structuring a final study or report. No surprise, therefore, that Giffney particularly applauds the ersatz infant observation experience of visitors to an art exhibition invited to cradle a hand-blown glass sculpture of a newborn baby.

She uses this example in introducing the value she attaches to seminars geared to raising the sensitivity of psychoanalytic trainees and practitioners to the immediate experience of the transference and countertransference in psychotherapy by getting them to attend to, and discuss in facilitator-led seminars, their immediate experience of particular cultural objects or works of art. She illustrates this in terms of seminars in which participants discuss their experience of photographs depicting psychoanalysts in their offices, of Frank O'Connor's short story My Oedipus Complex, Steve McQueen's film Shame, and of various pieces of music.

sue.einhorn@talk21.com

Sue Einhorn  

One of the great pleasures in reading this book was the many sibling memories it evoked in me. Perhaps it was not just the topic itself but also the straightforward

155

way the book is written and the author's use of both clinical and personal material. Being group-analytic and supporting a relational approach, I think that the reader is invited to co-construct the experience of the book as a parallel to the essence of the book, which is how sibling relationships are co-constructed within a family. It is a topic long overdue and the book brought back to my attention some long overdue memories!

In the Introduction we learn that the Sibling Matrix is ‘conceived as a transitional space between brothers and sisters, sustained through time in mutual memories, emotions, thoughts, phantasies or dreams - internal threads linking them to their shared roots and their sense of connectedness and belonging’ (p. 3). I do agree that the roots are shared and perhaps the belonging but, of course, each family member tends to remember things in their own way - through their individual matrix. This then is a good description of a group in which each person is free to be themselves whilst also belonging to the family group. It is this nurturing and tension that the author explores and how these experiences resonate in our relationships throughout our lives. What the book shows is the importance and power that siblings exert over each other but how overlooked that has been within the psychoanalytic community.

Both Freud and Foulkes lost sisters in the Holocaust and it may well have been the pain of such losses that moved them away from including siblings in their theoretical frameworks. However, it is perhaps even more of an issue for those of us interested in group therapy. In group analysis, the group itself is the therapist and ‘includes’ a conductor so that the conductor (analyst) is a group member, but with a special role. This means that power relations are always evolving and changing in our groups. All families have different power relations within them, which may evolve and change or get stuck. Inevitably, as the book shows, this includes sibling relationships which can be usefully echoed in member relationships in their therapy groups because they continue to permeate in all aspects of our lives.

Jan Hepburn  

As could be expected from a consummate Freud scholar, this book is larded with deep examination and interpretation of Freud's work in the areas of sexuality and the human condition. Rosine Perelberg sets out the basic position early. In the introduction, she describes Freud's assertion that humans have a drive which does not ‘correspond to any representation but is expressed through the repetition compulsion’ (p. 1). She goes on to say, ‘If the drives are at the root of psychic activity’ this inevitably means there is an excess which threatens to overwhelm the ‘psychic organisation’.

When Philip II of Macedon was busily warring around the Greek states in the 320s BCE and triumphing wherever he went, he sent a message to the Spartans saying if he invaded, they would be irrevocably destroyed (Ellis, 1976). The Spartans replied with the one word - ‘If’. Perelberg does not investigate the ‘if’ in this book to explore the different theories and perspectives on whether human beings are basically more drive driven or more object seeking. Fairbairn argued that the Freudian emphasis on drives and impulses was only half a story; in 1943 he wrote ‘the time is now ripe for a psychology of object-relationships’ (p. 60). Since then, probably more has been written, at least in the UK, about object relations than most other psychoanalytic subjects. Other than noting that for Klein ‘drives and objects are intrinsically linked’ (p. 78), however, Perelberg does not really enter into a discussion about these matters. What is on offer here is a Freudian-based understanding of human sexuality and of the work of psychoanalysis. On that basis, it is a tour de force.

The first part of the book describes the psychoanalytic understanding of the inherent bisexuality in all humans, and that, by definition, the power and force of these drives mean that sexuality is always in some way a trauma. Perelberg (p. 34) defines three terms - sex (‘a biological differentiation’), gender (‘a social construct’) and sexuality (‘unconscious phantasies … to do with desire, which is, by definition, perverse and polymorphous, excessive, disruptive, anxiety-provoking and always in conflict with the prohibition and the law against incest’). She states that it is sexuality which is ‘the object of psychoanalysis’ (p. 35). This section offers a coherent and explicit explanation of Freud's, and Perelberg's, thinking about sexuality. The understanding that sexuality always involves trauma because of the excess of feelings and sensations it produces, and the impossibility of their satisfaction with the parental objects, is clearly and unambiguously set out.

I recently heard a discussion between writer and broadcaster, Eliane Glaser, and Debra Myhill, director of the Centre for Research in Writing at the University of Exeter. They criticized the formulaic, abstruse learning of grammar by young children. If a child is unable to write a fluent sentence, I thought, is it because the idea of conjoining has not been sufficiently recognized, or could it point to a troubled ‘and’: perhaps between mummy and daddy? My mind turned to the book under review.

The book is divided into two sections. Part I comprises four previously unpublished lectures by Klein, dating from 1936 to 1939, supplemented by an autobiography written in 1959. The lectures show us Klein reaching out to educators, who ponder why some children find learning difficult. Part 2 comprises a series of papers (mostly published) based on the Melanie Klein Archive housed in the Wellcome Institute library. Jane Milton introduces the book and provides information on where in the Klein archive relevant material can be found.

Klein introduces educators to psychoanalytic concepts that could explain puzzling inhibitions of learning, especially the emotional dimension of what would otherwise seem to be cognitive deficiencies. She urges her audience to consider the unconscious dimension in children trying to be ‘normal’ but failing. Indeed, the child's unconscious awareness of adult discomfort urges the child to protect the adult, which unconsciously joins with the adult's reluctance to recognize the child's distress. The unfortunate interlocking of child and adult anxieties is part of the subtle relational environment in which children and their defences against anxiety develop. In an example, ‘the child is apt to feel that the “good” parents have changed into “bad” ones, or else that they will never come back because they are destroyed by his own greed and hatred’ (p. 48). The mother to whom he clings protects him from the phantasy, untrusted, feared, bad mother - also his bad self - as Klein will formulate as projective identification in 1946. In her many examples, Klein invites the parent or educator (in us) to see the internal dimension of the unconscious dimension of childhood terrors, including why they may be so puzzling to adults.

Diana Birkett  

In this quite polemical short book, Kohon makes a passionate plea for the unique qualities of psychoanalysis, and against the requirement for accountability that he feels is imposed by the mental health establishment. Though he reveres, and often quotes, Freud's genius in unravelling the workings of the unconscious, he sees his ‘misplaced ideals of scientism’ (p. 1) as partly responsible for capitulating to demands for proof of its effectiveness; and mounts a passionate defence of the single case study as the only way to demonstrate, rather than quantify, the specific workings of the psychoanalytic method.

To this end, he presents two extended pieces of work with two very different patients, whom he calls Tony and Barbara, to illustrate the complexity and unquantifiable nature of psychoanalysis. ‘If there are new psychoanalytic breakthroughs, whether theoretical or therapeutic, they emerge from the work carried out by the individual psychoanalyst in the consulting room with the patient’ (p. 7). Kohon underpins this approach with reference to quantum physics, quoting Carlo Rovelli's principle of indeterminacy, ‘a concept describing something that cannot be clearly defined or completely known’ (p. 3). He also enlists Thomas Kuhn's apparent shift from the famous idea of paradigms to that of ‘exemplars’, as the foundation of psychoanalytic training via the study of individual cases.

It would be difficult to do justice to the range and depth of Kohon's erudition in fields other than the psychoanalytic: he refers to philosophy, to modern physics, and to literature among other disciplines. But the core of his work is in assembling a range of references to the great tradition of psychoanalytic theorists, some of whom he sets against each other to enhance his central argument. Kohon's training in Argentina was largely Kleinian, and although Kleinian and post-Kleinian thinking permeates this work, he is open to some Laingian and Lacanian ideas, including untranslated French terms such as ‘bouffée délirante’ to describe psychotic episodes. He acknowledges Rosenfeld's adaptations of technique to explain some of his, as in the use of humour and cultural discussion in his relationship with Tony. In true classical tradition, however, he defends himself against the charge of using any corrective emotional experience, as opposed to transference interpretation, while acknowledging that the patient's transference remained an idealizing one to the end.

John Southgate 1934-2021

Brett Kahr

Brett Kahr

[kahr14@aol.com]

Brett Kahr  

On 24 April 2021, John Southgate, one of the United Kingdom's most creative and ground-breaking psychotherapists, died peacefully at the age of 86 years. A true pioneer of our profession, John championed both attachment theory and trauma theory, long before these arenas of thought had become standard practice. With his partner, Kate White, and a group of forward-thinking colleagues, he laid the foundations for the creation of The Bowlby Centre, named in honour of his much-cherished clinical supervisor, Dr John Bowlby, thus foregrounding the impact of early parent-infant attachment relationships and their long-term consequences.

Born in Carlton, Nottinghamshire, John Southgate grew up in a progressive, working-class, intercultural family, the only child of a Jewish mother and a Protestant father. After his schooling, Southgate worked for several years as a filing clerk and subsequently as a cost accountant, eventually enrolling in London's Garnett College at the age of 30, as a mature student. He subsequently earned a master's degree in management from the University of Sussex, and was soon appointed to lecture at the Polytechnic of North London (forerunner of London Metropolitan University), during which time he founded a blue-sky Diploma in Advanced Behavioural Science, teaching psychological theory to chief executive officers keen to enhance their understanding of workplace psychodynamics.

Southgate expanded his knowledge base by studying the writings of numerous forward-thinking psychoanalytical practitioners such as Dr Karen Horney, who championed not only a reconfiguration of female psychology but also the concept of ‘self analysis’. Southgate, steeped in Marxist theory, and the championship of equality, challenged the more elitist approach to psychoanalysis and began to develop the field of psychodynamically orientated peer counselling, thus making psychotherapeutic concepts more widely available at a time when few dared to speak about psychotherapy openly and in a non-shaming manner.

John Gale  

It would, perhaps, be an understatement to say that the past, especially Graeco-Roman antiquity and archaeology (digging up the past), interested Freud. As everyone knows, that which was ‘prior’, to use Ricoeur's idiom, was his main preoccupation (p. 37). During his eight years (1865 - 1873) at the Leopoldstädter Gymnasium, Freud studied Latin and Greek. There, one of his masters was the classics philologist Joseph Nahrhaft. In the university entrance examination, he had to translate from Greek to German 33 verses of Oedipus Rex and his translation was considered the best (Knoepfmacher, 1979). Some of his key ideas, however problematic they may seem to us now, he elucidated by turning to the Homeric tradition, to Sophocles, Virgil and other Greek and Latin literary sources. That is to say, despite a staunch belief in ‘science’, the path in thinking that Freud opened out was hermeneutic. As such, it was concerned, above all else, with texts. Thus, Freud, as Foucault put it ‘more than anyone brought the knowledge of man closest to its philological and linguistic model’ (Foucault, 1970, p. 361). Philology, of course, is founded, as it were, on the concept of the sēma (sign) and on notions of exegesis, ‘of signification, meaning: the array of methods elaborated by philologists …designed for the deciphering of texts’ (Forrester, 1980, p. 308). In some ways, it is this, more than anything else, that situates Freud's work firmly within the conceptual confines of the nineteenth century (Burrow, 1967). Such is, roughly, the territory through which Professor Lev Kenaan journeys in this volume.

Concerned largely with questions of methodology and the history of philology, in the first of the six sections that make up the book, the author skilfully weaves her way through a number of knotty issues in the fraught history of the relationship between the study of the classics and psychology. Psychological and psychoanalytic studies of the classics are, of course, notoriously naïve and Lev Kenaan more or less takes this as read, referring with concision to a couple of well-known studies, most notably one by Price (1990). Fair enough, given the circular arguments that characterize the psychologizing approach and their frequent mediocrity, it is easy to see why they are often derided. In considerably more detail, she discusses the use of psychoanalytic ideas by classicists, taking as a case example E.R. Dodds’ (1959) Greeks and the Irrational and its reception; and dreams, and more specifically to the use which Freud made, in his first major work (Die Traumdeutung), of Artemidorus. This suits, rather well, Lev Kenaan's ‘psychoanalytic hermeneutics’ and her concern to pay heed to the unconscious ‘as a principle of exegesis’ (p. 23 n. 38)

It is a well-known fact, well known to me anyway, that psychoanalysis is much like the Netherlands. No, I do not mean flat and dull but, rather, ‘pillarized’. In much of the late nineteenth century and most of the twentieth, Dutch society was typified by so-called pillars (‘zuilen’): Catholic, Calvinist or Social Democratic. You might go, say, to a Catholic school, then on to a Catholic university, join a Catholic trade union, read a Catholic newspaper, be ill in a Catholic hospital and so forth, barely ever meeting contemporaries doing the same thing in the Calvinist or Social Democratic pillars. It had the huge advantage of obviating potentially vicious social conflicts and the equally huge disadvantage of effectively institutionalizing them. The pillars began gradually to disintegrate in the later twentieth century as the bitter conflicts that had given rise to them came increasingly to seem ghostly to new generations, with new battles to fight.

COGNITIVE-BEHAVIOURAL THERAPY, INTERSUBJECTIVITY, KLEIN, NHS PSYCHOTHERAPY, QUALITATIVE RESEARCH, IAPT, INTERPRETERS, IPA

NHS therapists are required to work with interpreters. Therapy with an interpreter may take longer and aspects of the work may be challenging. Surveys of NHS mental health staff, particularly those working in Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) services, indicate that they are experiencing burn-out, low morale, and increasing stress and depression as a result of ever-increasing targets and workload demands. This study aimed to gain an understanding of the impact of the context of therapy on the experiences of therapists in the NHS of working with interpreters. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 qualified therapists working within an IAPT or secondary care psychology service from one NHS Trust. The verbal data were analysed using interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) methodology. The key finding of the study was that participants' experience of their organizational context (whether supportive or pressured and demanding) appeared to drive how they related to the interpreter. Previous literature has applied a psychoanalytic framework to understanding organizational, group and individual responses to stress in healthcare settings, including IAPT. Following the initial analysis, aspects of psychoanalytic theory were used to contextualize the findings. Epistemological and ethical tensions in making links to theoretical frameworks within an IPA study are acknowledged and discussed.

UTERUS, PRIMARY OBJECT, FEAR OF DEATH, ANXIETY, OBJECT RELATIONS

At birth, the newborn loses something that used to surround, protect, support and nurture it. Of course, we cannot yet speak of an object, but rather a part of the self being lost. This article describes how this lost part of the self, namely, the maternal uterus, gradually acquires the qualities of an object that can be represented, symbolized, introjected, projected and divided into good and bad. Its role in anxiety and especially in fears of death are emphasized, providing new possibilities for containing some of our patients’ most archaic fears. In such cases, where the primary object is charged with intense feelings of hate, fear and dependence, the analyst may find it difficult to relate to the patient as the Other and be good enough. Moreover, holding may trigger paranoid fears of entrapment. Implications of this concept for psychoanalytic practice are further discussed by including clinical material of two patients, a male and a female, suffering from extreme anxiety and panic attacks.

Joseph H. Berke 1939-2021

Morton Schatzman and Lois Elliott

Lois Elliott

[mortonschatzman@gmail.com]

[lois.elliott@blueyonder.co.uk]

Lois Elliott  

I first met my friend Joe in medical school at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York. He was uninterested in most of the medical subjects, except for psychiatry. A psychiatrist called John Thompson, who spent time sitting for hours with people labelled schizophrenic, just being there with them in silence, especially inspired him.

Joe was a medical doctor, a psychotherapist and author of many books. In 1965, he joined a community at Kingsley Hall in the East End of London, where Dr Ronald D. Laing and colleagues were setting up an important social experiment. The point was to see whether a drama of breakdown and ‘rebirth’ could help people with severe emotional damage. The first resident in the community, Mary Barnes, was a nurse whom Ronnie Laing described as having ‘turned her face to the wall’. Here, she had the good fortune to meet Joe, who helped guide her during and after her breakdown. Together, the two of them wrote Mary Barnes: Two Accounts of a Journey Through Madness.

When she was ‘down’, Mary began to paint for the first time. To make these paintings she smeared faeces with her fingers on the walls of her room. After 1967 she painted with oil on canvas, though she continued to use her fingers, and she sold many paintings. The playwright David Edgar wrote a play, Mary Barnes, based on the book, which was staged in 1978-79 at the Royal Court Theatre in London. Simon Callow played Eddie (a pseudonym for Joe) and Patti Love played Mary.

In 1970 Joe co-founded the Arbours Association with me and others. Arbours was set up in London as a charitable foundation, where people who might otherwise be in-patients in psychiatry wards could live communally. Arbours also had a training programme for psychotherapists, a low-cost psychotherapy clinic, and a crisis centre. For many years Joe was director of the crisis centre. Many therapists who worked there treasure it as a crucial experience in their education and training. He was also the Arbours representative on the British Journal of Psychotherapy editorial board in the early years of the BJP.

Dan Welldon BA MA MSc

Dan Welldon

Dan Welldon   Director of DW Pictures, London. He photographs a wide variety of subjects, mainly people, but also travel and architecture. He works with a wide range of commercial and editorial clients, agencies, and NGOs. Among other projects, he has photographed glaciers (‘From the Ends of the Earth’), and analysts' consulting rooms, including his mother's (‘Analytic Space’).

I describe the process by which I prepared to photograph my mother's deathbed scene. My researches led me to realize that a reluctance to document death is a very recent phenomenon. Famous deathbed paintings tended to be grand canvasses, or closer, more intimate paintings of the artist's loved ones. In capturing my mother's deathbed scene I chose a synthesis of these two styles, presenting a wider view of the scene in the tones of a textured palette of a painting, but with an intimate feel.

GRIEF, RAGE, LAST WORDS, THE NATURE OF CARE, CONTAGION

In this conference conversation, Lisa Appignanesi reads from her recently published memoir Everyday Madness: On Grief, Anger, Loss and Love, written after the death of her husband, the historian John Forrester. In the memoir she attempts to understand the grieving process and the rage that overtook her after his death. In conversation with the editor of the BJP, she comments on the symbolic import of ‘last words’, illness and death as forms of contagion, the nature of the caring relationship, and the way in which the dead inhabit us. The conversation moves on to the way in which her grandson's presence enables her gradually to move away from her rage, along with the birth of a second grandson - the arrival of new life. Comments from the floor, focusing on the nature of care, follow.

The Power of Music: Psychoanalytic Explorations by Roger Kennedy. Published by Phoenix Publishing House, Bicester, 2020; 192 pp, £24.99 paperback.

Andrea Sabbadini

Andrea Sabbadini

a.sabbadini@gmail.com

Andrea Sabbadini  

The subject of music spans an enormous territory, and the risk of any publication about it is that writers (and readers) will find themselves getting easily lost. In his latest book, Roger Kennedy has avoided this pitfall by focusing on an original and important theme, that of the power of music: where does this almost mysterious power originate, he wonders, how does it manifest itself, and why and how can music make composers, performers, and listeners feel empowered? By exploring such issues from different angles the book represents a valuable addition to the growing psychological and psychoanalytical literature on the complex relationship between music, bodily and mental - both cognitive and emotional - processes.

Gustav Mahler, in a letter to Lois Marshall, stated that ‘we find ourselves faced with the important question how, and indeed why music should be interpreted with words at all’ (quoted in Cooke, 1980, p. 54) - a rhetorical question also faced by many others, Kennedy himself included. If language is then inadequate to describe the beyond words musical experience, would this paradoxically make his book redundant? Not at all, of course, as the exploration of the reasons for such alleged incompatibility between musical and verbal languages, of how it manifests itself and what the respective functions of these two languages are in human lives, both personal and collective, is of great importance. Music, Kennedy explains, can ‘convey areas of experience that language cannot reach … [it] has the unique ability, unlike language, to convey simultaneously contrary emotions’ (pp. 6-7); ‘it does not have a clear object … nor an obvious narrative structure: [unlike verbal language] it is not representational’ (p. 11). Indeed, it may have a dreamlike quality: ‘one enters the dark world in which language and daily structures of time and causality no longer reign supreme’ (p. 15). Music allows us to lose ourselves in it ‘while also remaining ourselves; these are the moments of pleasurable illusion’ (p. 122) but can also evoke uncanny feelings of strangeness.

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[bjp@ann-scott.net]

Ann Scott  

We are delighted to be resuming publication of Clinical Commentaries following the appointment of our new editor for the section, Katya Orrell. Here we meet a patient in her early fifties, who grew up in poverty and had to take on adult responsibilities at an early age, who has been in once-weekly therapy for several years. The therapist reports ‘an overwhelming sense of stagnation’ in the work, ‘a sense of monotony and repetition’, while for the patient there is ‘emptiness, coldness and rejection’ during any silence. Our thought-provoking commentators take up different aspects of the situation, from contrasting theoretical perspectives. The patient may not have been able to use normal projective identification, her only recourse being to ‘attack the analyst with massive projective identification, resulting conversely in impairment of the analyst's ability to think’ (Konstantin Nemirovsky). Perhaps the therapy feels stuck ‘because the patient is bringing another person's pathology in place of her own’. The task then is to help her learn that ‘the therapist has another type of mind, one that is neutral and curious and that can support her to express deep pain safely’ (Emma Went). ‘With so many uses of the words “start” and “deliver”, in the patient's speech … one cannot help but think about the patient's early birth experiences and whether this woman's mother actually wished to “deliver” and permit her daughter to “start” her life’ (Brett Kahr).

Turning to our Theoretical Practice strand. Jan McGregor Hepburn searchingly re-evaluates Strachey's seminal work on the mutative interpretation, arguing that ‘the mutative interpretation continues to offer something potentially transformative’, but that the technique has to take account of ‘relational aspects of the treatment and the developmental issues of the patient’. Chris Brogan offers a meticulous examination of Winnicott's 1968 paper, ‘Sum, I am’, in the wider context of Winnicott's concept of unit status ‘and what might hamper this achievement’, recognizing Winnicott's ‘dazzling’ leaps of the imagination in the paper.

Konstantin Nemirovsky

Konstantin Nemirovsky

[k.nemirovsky@gmail.com]

Konstantin Nemirovsky  

‘I do not know where to start’ - the phrase, spoken by the patient at the beginning of the session, is both prologue and synopsis - an introduction to and essence of the patient's psyche. The parallel processes first described by Searles (1955) are

186

revealed to the reader. Trying in vain to understand the patient, one is confronted first with confusion and boredom, then with resentment and despair. The escape from this seemingly lifeless world becomes reverie, a means to what Bion called alpha-function. The first association that came to my mind was the recent story of the discovery of a 15 tonne plug (a fat-berg) in a London sewer. This was a solid mass of congealed used cooking oil, hygiene products and condoms which took several specialists plus two months of hard work to remove. I think one possible cause for the stagnation of the analytic process could be viewed as a similar ‘plug’ of beta-elements that have hardened and glued together in the patient's psyche, which is also brimming with uncontained fragments of inner experience. I will try to consider various factors that may have led to the formation of this pathological conglomerate, both in the patient's psyche and in the analytic process.

The poverty in which A. grew up was not only involving her external environment, but also her relational environment and mind. According to A., her childhood was mostly unhappy, filled with emotional deprivation, lack of safety and security as she was not allowed to simply ‘be a child’. She learned about hard work early and then became a good student, but it seems only to appease the insecurities and anxieties of her relatives. Although the story of A's later life presented here is sparse, we can assume that she was also unhappy in her adult life, doing only what seemed ‘right’. We know she sought therapy after repeated years of her trying to build a calm and secure life had failed. The patient was in her sixth decade, her children were presumably grown up, her husband had cheated on her, she had probably not succeeded in building a successful career or fulfilling herself in anything (at least not from what I understand of the description).

Dries Dulsster PHD , Stijn Vanheule PHD , Goedele Hermans MScs and Vicky Hennissen MScs

Vicky Hennissen   Clinical psychologist and PhD student at the Department of Psychoanalysis, Ghent University, Belgium.
LACAN, SUPERVISION, DIRECTION OF THE TREATMENT

This study aims at mapping and interpreting what is at stake in Lacanian psychoanalytic supervision. Using interview data of participants' personal accounts of supervision, the authors applied a thematic analysis to gain insight into what they believe are crucial components in these accounts of supervision. We interpret the data within the context of Lacan's text, ‘Direction of the Treatment and the Principles of its Power’, in which he articulates his conceptualization of psychoanalytic treatment. His views on interpretation (tactics), transference (strategy), and lack-of-being (politics) as the three elements that structure the actions of the analyst, guided our data-analysis. Participants indicate how their supervisor focuses on the symbolic dimension of speech, helping them avoid getting deceived by the dimension of the imaginary. During the supervision process, the supervisor does not respond from a master position, nor coach the supervisees. Supervisees develop their own style and framework for clinical work. Through discussing cases, supervisees learn to construct cases and focus on the singularity of the case, beyond structural diagnosis. Lastly, Lacanian supervisors only focus on the cases discussed, not on the person of the supervisee.

Psychodynamic Interventions in Pregnancy and Infancy: Clinical and Theoretical Perspectives by Björn Salomonsson. Published by Routledge, Abingdon and New York, 2018; £32.99 paperback.

Julie Kitchener

Julie Kitchener

[jkitchener22@gmail.com]

Julie Kitchener  

Björn Salomonsson takes guesswork seriously; the sort of attentive, informed guesswork a parent in ordinary good-enough circumstances might use in deducing and attending to a baby's needs. This same quality of ‘creative alertness’ (p. 16), which Salomonsson attributes to primary maternal preoccupation, pervades his latest book:

336

a rich and comprehensive exposition on the value of early psychotherapeutic interventions for infants and parents. He simply ‘cannot stop thinking’, he tells us, ‘what goes on in a baby's mind’. His answer - on the face of it a simple guide to anyone working in the field of perinatal mental health - is ‘to observe the baby, ask the mother, and guess’ (p. 165).

The reality, of course, is more complex. Salomonsson is a medical doctor, psychiatrist and adult and child psychoanalyst based in Stockholm. He has built an international reputation on his clinical, theoretical and research work in psychodynamic therapy with infants and parents (PTIP) at Child Health Centres. His own ‘guesswork’ - including his ‘imaginative formulations of the baby's or the parent's representations’ (p. xi) - is more a restless quest for understanding based on solid clinical experience, rigorous theoretical questioning and careful appraisal of the research evidence. Consequently, a bit like a baby, Psychodynamic Interventions is both irresistible and demanding.

Drawing the reader in with vivid case material from psychotherapeutic work with mothers, fathers and babies, the book details the unique psychic and emotional dynamics of pregnancy, childbirth, infancy and toddlerhood, weaving clinical insights, psychoanalytic theory and empirical evidence into an integrated, conceptually challenging (and occasionally dizzying) whole. Salomonsson's demand of his readers -be they psychoanalysts or psychotherapists, clinical psychologists or social workers, healthcare workers, medics or research scientists - is that they too are willing to engage with creative alertness. He wants us to come to our own conclusions about the validity of his arguments and then let these ‘inspire - or not’ our work (p. 7).

John Gale

John Gale

[johngaleuk@gmail.com]

John Gale  

The curious title of this book immediately confronts us with a number of questions, many of which have received considerable attention over the years. Does schizophrenia exist? If so, is it an illness? Is it something that can be ‘resolved’? What is the relationship between psychiatry and psychoanalysis? Is there a psychoanalytic view of schizophrenia and the relationship between psychiatry and psychoanalysis, or a number of different views within the various psychoanalytic schools and traditions? Although the author does not discuss in any detail these underlying issues directly, it would be a mistake to imagine that she does not take up a position in regard to them. One reason why it is important to say this is because the complex history of madness - in its varying forms - shows how difficult it is to pin the concept down as it shifts across a series of intersecting intellectual landscapes. Thus, answers to the question ‘What is madness?’ vary considerably depending not only on the discourse within which the question is posed but also on when one asks the question. In other words, our understanding of madness is closely linked to what Wittgenstein (1953) called its ‘language game’ as well as to its chronology. Not only within this chronology do we find gradual changes in its meaning, but also key moments at which what it means to be mad is dramatically re-conceptualised. Indeed, different insanities not only emerge and disappear, they also coexist. Still others re-appear in new guises. Yet all of them are closely related to questions of belief and power. The power both of individuals - for example, the healer in antiquity, the priest or the doctor - and of the shifting influence of institutions such as the Church, medicine, and pharmaceutical companies. And a belief that ‘truth’ is disclosed in the discourse, whether that be conceived allegorically or literally.

Rozsika Parker Prize 2021

The British Journal of Psychotherapy's Prize established in 2013 in memory of Rozsika Parker focuses on a critical engagement with questions of creativity. An influential art historian and clinician, Rozsika Parker represented WPF/FPC on the BJP's Board for many years and was well known for her commitment to creativity, in both art and clinical practice. The Prize has two entry routes: a Student Path and a Post-Qualification Path. Students or qualified clinicians are invited to submit original papers on adult, child, couple, or group psychotherapy or psychoanalysis, on clinical, theoretical, applied or research topics. It is expected that authors will address the question of creativity in their submission, however broadly conceived. This may be implicit or explicit. In addition to the focus on creativity, the application of psychoanalytic theory to questions of gender; the arts; and social and cultural themes is welcomed. Authors should also consult the BJP's submission guidelines, particularly in relation to confidentiality and consent. Any clinical material must be fully anonymized, with disguise of any biographical details. The work should be prepared with the Journal's Aims and Scope statement in mind. Advice will be available for questions concerning confidentiality, or eligibility to submit work.

The Student path is open to students on an initial psychodynamic psychotherapy or clinical psychology or psychoanalytic psychotherapy training leading to a clinical qualification, who are either currently in training or who have qualified within the last 12 months; and to students on university courses in psychoanalytic studies, and on university courses where psychoanalysis is a significant component. The Post-Qualification path is open to clinically qualified individuals only. A paper that has only been made available to an institution's membership (for example, in an internal bulletin) is eligible to be entered into the competition, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers (Student or Post-Qualification) may have been submitted as part of the requirements of a programme of study, if this is acceptable to the author's course team, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers should be singly authored, but due acknowledgement should be made if the work is based on a joint project. Manuscripts should be between 4000 and 6000 words in length including references, not including an Abstract of 200 words which should head the paper. The word length must be stated on the title page. The author's name should not appear anywhere in the body of the paper. If the paper is based on or makes use of the author's earlier published work this should be acknowledged in the form ‘(Author, date)’ within the text (i.e. the word ‘Author’ is given, plus date of publication) and there should be no entry in the References list. Manuscripts should be sent as a Word attachment to Ann Scott, Editor-in-Chief, c/o the BJP's Editorial Administrator bjpsychotherapyadmin@wiley.com

Ros Howell

Ros Howell

[rosalindhowell74@gmail.com]

Ros Howell   Graduated from Brighton University in psychodynamic psychotherapeutic counselling in 2020 where a version of this essay was submitted as coursework. She now practices at Brighton Therapy Centre and is a member of BACP. In 2008 she obtained an MA in dance movement psychotherapy from Goldsmiths and is a member of the Association for Dance Movement Psychotherapy (ADMP). She edits the arts reviews section for Transformations (the journal for Psychotherapists and Counsellors for Social Responsibility - PCSR).
TEMPORALITY, TIME, EMBODIED COUNTERTRANSFERENCE, TRAUMA, SPACE, INTERRUPTION, SOCIO-POLITICAL, LABAN MOVEMENT ANALYSIS

Our relationship to time is both a developmental and a relational one; an inter- and intra-psychic experience. Exploring how the theories of Freud, Klein, Winnicott, and their successors offer explanations of how the psychoanalytic subject develops and sustains a concept of time and the factors that may hinder this, this essay suggests that different qualities of time, such as continuity, rhythm, repetition and interruption, can reveal themselves through the client's transferential and countertransferential relationship with the therapist. Using fictionalized clinical examples it explores how a bodily felt experience of time was thought about by the therapist/author using Laban movement analysis to support a client in ‘working through’ early material that felt stuck. The exploration of a client's perspective is brought in through the writings of the activist Passerini on her psychoanalytic treatment (cited by Baraitser in Enduring Time) and her experience of trauma's capacity to stop time. The essay also looks at how psychoanalytic ideas of temporality challenge the ‘recruiting’ of time by the wider culture to create more time-efficient late-capitalist subjects but by using ideas from movement studies and a Lacanian influenced time register it is suggested that cultural attacks on subjective experiences of temporality could be challenged within therapy. It is hoped the essay encourages the therapist to become alert to the manifestations of different temporal experiences within the therapeutic relationship and to develop a creative, embodied language with which to explore it with the client.

Agnieszka Zalewska   Sociologist and a psychoanalytic psychotherapist, registrant of the British Psychoanalytic Council. She is a clinician working in a South-West England Step-4 NHS psychotherapy department, as well as in a gender identity clinic and private practice. TRANSGENDER IDENTITY, FANTASY, ADULT PSYCHOTHERAPY, TRANSFERENCE/COUNTERTRANSFERENCE, AUTISTIC SPECTRUM DISORDER, BODY, MIND

This article presents clinical work with a transgender patient who was attending a regional NHS gender clinic in England. It aims to link aspects of the patient's identity formation with the theoretical framework offered by the French psychiatrist and psychoanalyst Piera Aulagnier. Emphasizing the complexity of (gender) identity and its process of development, the concept of the ‘birth of the body’ is used to situate the development of gender identity as a process of the creation of an individual narrative, with the experience of embodiment based on unconscious fantasy as specifically troubling for transgender individuals. This struggle may be seen in the clinical material presented. Recommendations are made for working with transgender clients who suffer from a disturbance in creating and navigating relationships. By using the concept of the ‘word-bearer’, an exploration may be opened up of the unconscious dynamics between the clinic as an object that offers understanding, and the service user who is seeking meaning and a remedy for subjective suffering.
